Q: How to use match case with a class type A:

How about using an if guard in the relevant cases?

class Class1():
    pass

class Class2():
    pass

def f(obj: Class1 | Class2 | type[Class1] | type[Class2]) -> None:
    match obj:
        case Class1():
            print("Class1 instance")
        case Class2():
            print("Class2 instance")
        case cls if cls is Class1:
            print("Class1 type")
        case cls if cls is Class2:
            print("Class2 type")
        case _:
            print("???")

f(Class1())
f(Class2())
f(Class1)
f(Class2)

# output:
Class1 instance
Class2 instance
Class1 type
Class2 type

Reference: See the Adding conditions to patterns section of PEP 636.

Q: How to manage platform-specific UI and shared logic in MAUI Hybrid without "spaghetti code"? A:

MVVM is most definitely the answer for a UI platform like MAUI that supports data binding rather than direct access to controls. The premise behind that design pattern is that there is such clean separation between the UI and the business logic / services in the Model and ViewModel layers, that in theory you could replace the entire UI with a console window and create a working application. Ok, so it wouldn't look pretty or be at all user friendly, but you could still display any data required as supplied by the ViewModel and use commands to trigger processing actions from the UI to other layers of the application.

The SOLID principles will help to prevent spaghetti code - in particular keep classes small and focused on a single task, and structuring applications using interfaces rather than specific class implementations.

There will be differences between Android and iOS applications, but that should be purely in the UI layer, or a few operating system specific tasks. That's why MAUI will create separate UI projects within the solution for each platform, but the remaining code will be shared between them.

Q: Strange behavior of the EAX register being truncated to 16-bit when single-stepping with CodeViewer debugger? A:

Thanks to @PeterCordes for the helpful tips.

If you use step-by-step debugging a program in CodeViewer and use the EAX register in your code, then the upper half of the 16 bits becomes zero. The data is crack. You can't see how your code is actually executed. For example, your data in EAX from 0x08000140 (132,218,048 in decimal) is converted to 0x00000140 (320 in decimal).

Do not use CodeViewer to debug code with 32-bit registers. For example, you can use lDebug. Use the rx option for view 32 bits registers.
